analysis.one_liner: Lets financial firms earn fees selling investments to 401(k) savers while advising those same savers.
analysis.headline: The Senate never voted on the bill: it was introduced March 1, 2002, referred to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, and died there when the Congress ended January 3, 2003.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal pension law generally forbids an adviser from recommending an investment while pocketing fees from selling it. This bill would carve out an exception: banks, insurers, brokers, and investment advisers could legally give retirement advice to 401(k) participants and then earn fees on the transactions that follow, as long as they disclose their fees and conflicts in writing and meet other conditions. It also shields employers who hire such advisers from liability for the specific advice given to workers.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers with 401(k) plans gain access to professional investment advice they may not otherwise get, under new written-disclosure rules. Financial firms — brokers, banks, insurers, investment advisers and their affiliates — gain a large new permitted business: advising plan participants and then collecting fees, including from third parties, on sales that follow from that advice.

how_it_helps.text: The bill creates a legal pathway, now barred by pension law, for regulated financial firms to give investment advice to 401(k) participants and beneficiaries [S2].

Advisers must disclose all fees and compensation, including third-party payments, any interest they or affiliates hold in recommended investments, and any limits on their advice, in writing understandable to the average participant [S2][S3].

Advisers must acknowledge in writing that they are acting as a fiduciary of the plan, transactions must occur only at the participant's direction, and terms must be at least as favorable as an arm's-length deal [S2][S3].
Employers who arrange for a fiduciary adviser are excused from monitoring the specific advice given, while keeping the duty to prudently select and periodically review the adviser [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: If it passed, 401(k) savers would bear the cost of advice that is legally permitted to be conflicted — the adviser's profit can rise with the products it recommends. Plan assets could be used to pay for the advice, so participants may bear fees directly. Employers' reduced monitoring duty shifts the risk of bad specific advice onto workers.

drawbacks.text: The bill authorizes the exact conflict ERISA's prohibited-transaction rules exist to prevent: the same firm can recommend a security and collect fees, including from third parties, on its sale [S2][S3].

Employers who hire a fiduciary adviser have no duty to monitor the specific advice given to individual workers, so a worker who receives poor advice has a harder time holding the employer responsible [S2][S3].
The protections rely heavily on disclosure — fees, affiliations, and limits on advice must be stated in writing — and disclosure alone does not remove the sales incentive behind the advice [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The case for the bill is real: many 401(k) savers get no professional advice at all, and the bill attaches fiduciary status and disclosure duties to any advice it permits. But the core bargain is that financial firms get a new revenue stream built on a conflict of interest, policed mainly by paperwork, and employers are insulated from monitoring the advice itself. An honest supporter would have to acknowledge that the participant's protection depends on disclosures most savers won't read closely.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate's health and labor committee on the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and it died when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Tim Hutchinson introduced the bill in the Senate on March 1, 2002, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and PENSIONS the same day [S5].
That was the bill's last action: no markup, no committee vote, and no floor vote ever occurred before the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003 [S5].
The bill had a sponsor and 3 Republican cosponsors, but no committee consideration was ever scheduled [S4][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, 401(k) savers kept the stricter conflict-of-interest rules, and financial firms did not get the new fee-earning advice business it would have opened up.

for.name: Sen. Tim Hutchinson
for.role: U.S. Senator from Arkansas, bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill in the Senate on March 1, 2002.

against.name: HELP Committee
against.role: Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and never held a markup or vote on it; it died in committee.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's sponsor and all 3 cosponsors were Republicans, but it never reached a vote, so no roll-call record shows where Democrats or the broader Senate stood.

industries.note: The bill would let broker-dealers give retirement advice while earning fees — including third-party payments — on the securities they recommend, turning a conflict of interest into a permitted business. Savers' account balances are what that business feeds on.

Both are named as qualifying fiduciary advisers, opening the 401(k) advice market to them and allowing compensation on resulting transactions. Their gain comes through fees attached to workers' retirement savings.

Registered investment advisers also qualify as fiduciary advisers and gain a clearer legal path to serve 401(k) participants for fees. Fee-for-service advisers profit alongside savers who want advice.

Plan sponsors are exempted from monitoring the specific advice an outside adviser gives to workers, reducing their legal exposure. The savings come at the expense of the worker, who has no employer backstop for the advice itself.
